verdicts.text: Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications; its constructs are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation; once stable, Ion will be released as SST v3.
verdicts.evidence: SST's Jan 2024 post says "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications" and "Once Ion is stable, it'll be released as SST v3," so the attribution is faithful to the original. But SST's Aug 2024 post says "Ion is now officially being released as SST v3," which means the future tense ("will be released") is now out of date.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the source's Jan-2024 plan ("Once Ion is stable, it'll be released as SST v3") is presented as still pending, but it shipped in Aug 2024. The source also says components are "defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi"; the claim leaves out the Terraform-providers part.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The future-tense wording is stale by about 2 years. pulumi/docs#21673 already proposes rewriting this FAQ answer to say Ion shipped as v3.

verdicts.text: AWS CDK tied infrastructure to AWS; debugging CDK was frustrating due to CloudFormation templates; multi-cloud with CDK was nearly impossible.
verdicts.evidence: The factual core holds up. Pulumi's CDK comparison page says CDK "transpiles programs into AWS CloudFormation templates that the AWS CloudFormation service deploys, and supports AWS only." The rest ("debugging was frustrating", "multi-cloud was nearly impossible") describes SST's own experience in a customer case study and can't be checked against product source.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim retells SST's experience (the post's embedded talk, L91), not a technical spec. Only the AWS-only / CloudFormation-synthesis part is checkable. The only corroboration is another pulumi.com page, which can back the claim up but isn't independent authority.

verdicts.text: Multi-cloud was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Independent sources say AWS CDK targets AWS only, which supports the claim's characterization. Encore: "CDK is AWS only. If you deploy to GCP or Azure, CDK doesn't help." SST's own coverage presents cross-provider (multi-cloud) linking as new with the move to Pulumi, something the CDK-based versions couldn't do.
verdicts.framing_note: This is an editorial judgment ("nearly impossible"), not something a source states outright. It is consistent with CDK being AWS-only. CDKTF, a separate tool, did offer multi-cloud, but AWS CDK itself did not.

verdicts.text: In its early days, SST was built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own blog says "We are working on a new version of SST that's not based on CDK," and a third-party write-up says "the first two versions of SST were basically the wrappers and enhancers of AWS CDK." AWS CDK does support TypeScript and Python, along with Java, C#, and Go.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim names only TS/Python out of CDK's languages, which is fine because 'which' refers to CDK. SST v2 itself only worked with JS/TS, so a reader could wrongly think SST supported Python.
verdicts.intuition_flag: 'TypeScript or Python' could be misread as describing SST, which only supported JS/TS, even though CDK itself supported both.

verdicts.text: AWS CDK allows developers to define their infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The AWS CDK v2 guide confirms that TypeScript and Python are both supported: "first-class support for the TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Java, C#, and Go general-purpose programming languages." The claim is true, but it lists only two of the six supported languages.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Saying "TypeScript or Python" may make readers think CDK supports only those two, when it also supports JavaScript, Java, C#, and Go. Consider rewording to "languages such as TypeScript or Python".

verdicts.text: AWS CDK and CloudFormation act as code generators producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources, so the code the developer writes is not the code running during deployment.
verdicts.evidence: This is accurate for CDK. Pulumi's CDK comparison page says: "running `cdk synth` produces an AWS Cloud Assembly — CloudFormation JSON or YAML templates plus other deployment assets — which is uploaded to Amazon S3/ECR and deployed by the AWS CloudFormation service." That matches how AWS documents CDK synthesis, but I didn't fetch AWS's own docs in this session.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The wording is loose: CloudFormation isn't a code generator. It runs the templates. Only the CDK code generates them, so the pairing "CDK and CloudFormation act as code generators" is slightly off.

verdicts.text: Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment instead of generating an intermediary format.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's architecture guide says that on `pulumi up` "the Pulumi CLI launches the ... language host and requests that it execute the program," and that the program sends resource registration requests straight to the deployment engine while it runs. No intermediate template (such as the CloudFormation template CDK synthesizes) is produced.

verdicts.text: The Founding Engineer at SST said: 'With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle.'
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) I found no independent source for this quote. The only places it turned up were the reviewed blog post's own live page (pulumi.com/blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/), which can't verify itself, and nowhere else I searched. It likely comes from the PulumiUP 2024 talk "From CDK to Pulumi: Evolution of SST". A Pulumi page lists Dax Raad in that talk as "Founding Engineer, SST", which supports the title, but I couldn't find a transcript to check the quote word for word.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran queries "SST Pulumi \"natural extension of writing code\" founding engineer", "Dax Raad Pulumi \"intuitive and powerful\" deployment \"natural extension\"", "SST case study Pulumi quote \"traditional IaC tools can't handle\""; the only match was the reviewed page itself. https://www.pulumi.com/blog/pulumiup-global-cloud-iac-platform-engineering-ai-conference/ supports the speaker's title only.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim names a speaker (SST's Founding Engineer), not a linked source. The quote probably comes from the PulumiUP 2024 talk, but no transcript was available to check against.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The post attributes the quote to a role, not a name, and its polished marketing tone ("advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle") suggests it may be paraphrased from the talk rather than quoted exactly. The author should confirm it word for word against the PulumiUP recording.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Insights (product page) provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities for deployments.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The visibility part holds up. Pulumi's docs describe Insights as providing "comprehensive cloud visibility and policy enforcement—discover all infrastructure and ensure compliance," and the overview says it "provides advanced search, analytics, and AI for your infrastructure as code." None of the sources I found describe it as a tool for debugging deployments. They present it as resource discovery, search, analytics and policy compliance.
verdicts.source: https://www.pulumi.com/docs/insights/ ; https://www.pulumi.com/docs/insights/concepts/ (WebSearch ran query "Pulumi Insights product page")
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: the source says 'cloud visibility / search, analytics' of resources, but the claim adds 'debugging capabilities for deployments', which no Insights source describes. Deployment debugging fits better with Pulumi Cloud update logs and Deployments.
verdicts.intuition_flag: 'Debugging for deployments' sounds like a generic LLM-style description of Insights, not how the product actually positions itself.

verdicts.text: Pulumi has built-in extensibility features including custom providers and dynamic components.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi does document custom providers and "dynamic providers" ("The dynamic resource provider construct can be used to build a local provider... lighter weight than custom providers"), plus component resources. But I found no Pulumi feature called "dynamic components": the term seems to blend dynamic providers and component resources.
verdicts.framing_note: The general idea (Pulumi is extensible through custom providers) is right, but "dynamic components" doesn't match any Pulumi term. It should probably say "dynamic providers" or "component resources".
verdicts.intuition_flag: "dynamic components" isn't a Pulumi term. It's likely an LLM blend of "dynamic providers" and "components".

verdicts.text: With CDK/CloudFormation, SST had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to customize deployments.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own "Moving away from CDK" post says the CDK community, SST included, has to "rely on this [Custom Resources] for basically anything that isn't supported." It also says CDK "has to create these hacks to work around it" and that SST "adds a hack to unwind the damage caused by that hack." The post notes that Custom Resources run on Lambda functions.
verdicts.framing_note: This is a paraphrase. The source says SST relied on Lambda-backed Custom Resources and hacks to handle unsupported functionality, which matches the claim's "hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions."

verdicts.text: Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments from one workflow.
verdicts.evidence: The languages overview says "Pulumi supports TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go, .NET, Java, YAML, and HCL," so the four languages the claim names are all supported. The same page's description mentions AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. On-premises support rests on general knowledge of registry providers such as vSphere, OpenStack, and Kubernetes, which I didn't check in this session.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim names only 4 of the 8 supported languages. Naming a subset is still accurate.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Cloud Deployments (docs page) supports advanced deployment workflows.

That page describes Pulumi Deployments as running "`pulumi up`, `preview`, `refresh`, and `destroy`... on demand, in response to version control events, on a schedule, or through the REST API." The docs home also lists "drift detection and remediation, ephemeral review stacks for pull requests, scheduled operations, and TTL-based cleanup," which supports the loose phrase "advanced deployment workflows."
verdicts.framing_note: The claim's "advanced deployment workflows" is a vague summary. The linked page's specific features (git triggers, schedules, drift remediation, review stacks) cover it.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The blog sentence says SST will build workflows "building on Pulumi's extensibility" (e.g. rollback, faster deploys) but links to the managed Deployments service. That link context is a bit loose, but it isn't a factual error.

verdicts.text: Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.

So the fact is right, but the sentence still describes a future event that took place about two years ago.

verdicts.text: SST leverages Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own providers doc says: "SST is built on Pulumi/Terraform and **supports 150+ providers**". It also points to Pulumi registry pages for provider configuration and to "the Pulumi docs" for provider functions. That supports SST running on Pulumi, with Terraform-derived providers reached through Pulumi. The doc doesn't use the word "bridging", though.
verdicts.framing_note: Source says 'built on Pulumi/Terraform' and links Pulumi registry provider docs. The claim reads this as Pulumi engine plus Terraform providers bridged through Pulumi, which fits but is spelled out more explicitly than the source.

verdicts.text: SST makes money primarily through its managed service called SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own pricing post says the Console is optional ("You don't need the Console to use SST") and has a free tier ("Workspaces with 350 active resources or fewer"). Above that tier, the Console bills $0.086 per active resource. The "primarily" revenue point is only confirmed indirectly: the Console is SST's one visible paid product, and a single third-party page says SST "generates revenue predominantly from its managed service."
verdicts.framing_note: No official SST page found that says outright the Console is its main source of revenue. That part is inferred from the Console being SST's only paid offering.

verdicts.evidence: This is the blog post's own publication date in its front matter. It is metadata the author sets, not a factual assertion that an outside source could confirm or refute.

verdicts.text: In SST's deploy chain, SST components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, and the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's concepts docs describe the engine's role: "The deployment engine computes the set of operations needed to drive the current state of your infrastructure into the desired state expressed by your program," and say resource properties "are also used between resources to handle any necessary dependencies." I couldn't check the claim that SST components compile into Pulumi resources against SST's own source in this lane. It does fit the SST docs the post quotes ("SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine").
verdicts.framing_note: The docs say "current state"; the claim says "actual state". Without a refresh, Pulumi diffs against the state it has recorded, not the live cloud, so "actual" is a small simplification.

verdicts.text: SST stores deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account, not in Pulumi Cloud.
verdicts.evidence: SST's state docs say: "The state is generated locally but is backed up to your provider using: 1. A **bucket** to store the state, typically named `sst-state-<hash>`. This is created in the region of your `home`." The `home` setting can be `aws` or `cloudflare`, so the S3 bucket is where state goes with the AWS home. SST does not use Pulumi Cloud for this.
verdicts.framing_note: Source says state goes to a bucket in your `home` provider ("Currently `aws` and `cloudflare` are supported"). The claim covers only the AWS case, where that bucket is S3 in the user's account.

verdicts.text: The SST team has repeatedly described, since the rewrite shipped, that SST's architecture is built on the Pulumi engine.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own v3 announcement (Aug 2024) says they built "a new deployment engine that would use Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation." A third-party write-up from 2025 also says SST's documentation "explicitly notes that SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine," so SST has said this more than once since v3 shipped.
verdicts.framing_note: SST describes its engine as "Pulumi and Terraform" (Terraform providers bridged through Pulumi, deployed by Pulumi). The claim says only "the Pulumi engine," which fits because Pulumi is the deployment engine. "Repeatedly" is backed by the v3 post plus the SST docs, as reported by a third party.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Repeatedly described since the rewrite shipped" is vague. I could only confirm two SST-owned statements (the v3 post and the docs), and the docs one only through a third party.

verdicts.text: SST apps define infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST components (functions, queues, buckets, static sites), and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.

verdicts.intuition_flag: "Actual state" is a bit loose. By default the engine diffs against the state it last recorded, not live cloud state; it only reads live state if you run a refresh. The claim may be overstating here.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's Terraform bridge translates each resource into cloud API calls via Terraform-bridged providers in SST.
verdicts.evidence: The cited repo returns HTTP 200 and describes itself as "A library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi." That supports the claim's core point. The fetched text is truncated to the title, so it doesn't say anything about SST or about how API calls are made.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says "allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi." The claim says the bridge "translates each resource into cloud API calls via Terraform-bridged providers in SST." Strictly, the bridged Terraform provider makes the API calls and the bridge adapts it. That's a loose simplification, not a wrong fact.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The wording treats the bridge as the part that makes the cloud API calls. Actually, the bridge wraps Terraform providers and the providers make the calls.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's engine handles dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and the plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs, while SST owns the CLI, component model, and local dev loop.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's official docs say "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine," with Terraform providers bridged through Pulumi. That covers Pulumi handling dependency resolution, preview/diff, state, and providers. SST's docs also describe its own CLI, built-in higher-level components, and dev experience. This split is how SST itself describes the arrangement, though no source spells out every item in the claim's list.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Hundreds of provider APIs" stretches SST's own count: "SST is built on Pulumi/Terraform and supports 150+ providers." Consider "150+" instead.

verdicts.text: AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
verdicts.evidence: AWS said CloudFormation already supported "over 900 resource types" in April 2022. A current third-party index lists "all 1613 AWS CloudFormation resource types across 280 services." So "hundreds" works as a lower bound, but it understates the real count, which is well over a thousand.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim cites no source. "Hundreds" is a vague lower bound, and the real count (~1,600 CFN types) satisfies it.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Hundreds" undersells it: AWS now has more than 1,000 resource types (~1,600 in CloudFormation), so the author might want "over a thousand".

verdicts.text: Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi state docs name two backend classes: Pulumi Cloud and a "DIY backend" that stores state in "an object store you manage—AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, ... a PostgreSQL database, or your local filesystem." They also say "Pulumi's SDK works with all backends," so the engine runs without a Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Any Pulumi-hosted service" is absolute. By default the CLI may download provider plugins from get.pulumi.com and check for updates, so it is only strictly true with plugins pre-installed or mirrored.

verdicts.text: The blog post /blog/any-terraform-provider/ and docs page /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/ and /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/ exist as cross-referenced targets.
verdicts.evidence: I found all three link targets in the repo: the blog post content/blog/any-terraform-provider/index.md (title "Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi"), the page content/docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers.md (title "Use Terraform Providers"), and the page content/docs/iac/concepts/automation-api.md (title "Automation API").

verdicts.text: Pulumi's Automation API lets teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools, and the provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
verdicts.evidence: The cited repo describes itself as "A library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi." That makes it a tool for provider authors who build bridged providers. It does not say that any Pulumi user can consume Terraform providers directly. The page also says nothing about the Automation API half of the sentence.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the source says 'a library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi' (for provider authors), but the claim says it 'lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly' (end-user direct consumption, which fits the separate any-Terraform-provider feature better). The Automation API part isn't covered by this citation.

verdicts.text: The blog post /blog/any-terraform-provider/ exists and describes the provider bridge.
verdicts.evidence: The page https://www.pulumi.com/blog/any-terraform-provider/ is live, titled "Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi". It says "Pulumi now supports using any Terraform or OpenTofu provider with Pulumi" and explains that Terraform providers are just a standard resource model with CRUD operations, which is what Pulumi bridges.
verdicts.framing_note: The page exists and is about using any Terraform/OpenTofu provider through Pulumi's bridge. The search snippet did not contain the exact phrase "provider bridge," but the topic matches.

verdicts.text: Nitric, Defang, and SST all expose a narrower, more opinionated interface to their users while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Nitric docs: "All of Nitric's core providers AWS, GCP and Azure are powered by Pulumi" (via the Automation API). Defang's CD program "receives a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs pulumi up", and SST v3 (Ion) is built on Pulumi. Calling them "narrower, more opinionated" is the author's own description. The "provider bridge" part is an inference: it holds only because pulumi-aws and similar providers are bridged, and no source says it directly.
verdicts.framing_note: Sources show each tool deploys through the Pulumi engine or Automation API. The "provider bridge" detail is inferred and not stated in any source. Nitric also allows Terraform-based providers, but its core providers run on Pulumi.

verdicts.text: Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code; they work entirely in SST's component model.
verdicts.evidence: Sources support the idea that SST components wrap Pulumi (fireup.pro: "You only touch Pulumi directly if you need a resource SST doesn't yet provide"). But no SST or Pulumi source gives any usage data showing that "most" SST users never write Pulumi code.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "SST v3 components built on Pulumi users don't need to know Pulumi"; https://fireup.pro/news/modern-web-development-ion-the-sst-deployment-engine; https://sst.dev/docs/components/
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Most SST users" is a claim about a user population with no source behind it. SST docs also openly encourage using Pulumi providers directly and $transform with Pulumi args, so the "never write a line" wording may overstate things. Consider softening it to "many SST users" or "you don't need to write Pulumi code".

verdicts.text: Because SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources, resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own docs (all-providers.mdx, base64-decoded) say: "Aside from the built-in components, SST supports any of the 150+ Pulumi and Terraform providers." They also say: "Once added, you can use a resource from the provider in your `sst.config.ts`… since the AWS provider comes preloaded, you can use any AWS resource directly as well," with a raw `new aws.apprunner.Service(...)` inside the app's `run` function.
verdicts.framing_note: The source confirms you can use raw Pulumi provider resources in the same sst.config.ts app. It doesn't say the ability exists *because* constructs compile to Pulumi resources, but it describes the same architecture, so the claim holds.

verdicts.text: The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
verdicts.evidence: The cited page (HTTP 200) is OpenCode's homepage. It never mentions the `sst` npm package or weekly downloads, only OpenCode's own stats: "With over 208,000 GitHub stars, 950 contributors, and over 13,000 commits, OpenCode is used and trusted by over 16M developers every month." The link looks like the wrong target for this figure, and npm's download stats would be the right source.
verdicts.framing_note: Wrong target: the cited page is about OpenCode, not about sst npm downloads.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The exact weekly count (796,291) needs an npm downloads API source (api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/2026-09-05:2026-09-11/sst), not opencode.ai. Also check that the 2026 week has actually happened and isn't a future date.

verdicts.text: opencode (anomalyco/opencode) has a larger following on GitHub than SST itself, and has grown quickly since launch.
verdicts.evidence: The cited URL returned HTTP 200, but the pre-fetched body was cut off after the title "GitHub - anomalyco/opencode: The open source coding agent." It contains no star or follower counts and no growth data, and there is nothing on SST to compare against.
verdicts.framing_note: The fetched page only confirms the repo exists. It doesn't support the comparative claim ("larger following than SST") or the growth claim.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Star counts for opencode and SST change over time, so a comparison and a "grown quickly" claim can go stale. Check the current counts of both repos (sst/sst vs anomalyco/opencode).

verdicts.text: SST's framework dependency on the Pulumi engine hasn't changed as a result of the team also working on opencode, and SST is not being abandoned.
verdicts.evidence: SST's current docs still say "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine," so the dependency on Pulumi hasn't changed. On whether SST is abandoned, third-party sources say it is "Maintenance mode, not dead... active development shifted to OpenCode" and that "critical fixes still ship," so "not abandoned" holds.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Several third-party sources describe SST as in "maintenance mode" since 2025, with active development moved to OpenCode. The post's wording, "a legitimate expansion of what the team works on," may make SST's status sound better than it is. The reviewer should consider saying it is in maintenance mode.

verdicts.text: If you run SST, you are running Pulumi's engine whether or not you've written any Pulumi code.
verdicts.evidence: SST's go.mod (sst/sst, now anomalyco/sst, dev branch) lists direct dependencies on `github.com/pulumi/pulumi/pkg/v3 v3.215.0` and `github.com/pulumi/pulumi/sdk/v3 v3.215.0`, so the SST CLI embeds Pulumi's engine packages to deploy the TypeScript components users write in sst.config.ts. That confirms the claim for current SST (v3). I checked the dependency manifest, not the deploy code path itself.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is only true for SST v3 (Ion). SST v2 and earlier were built on AWS CDK/CloudFormation, so "if you run SST" is too broad unless the post says it means v3.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state, policy as code provides central guardrails, and Pulumi components enable sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
verdicts.evidence: The /docs/iac/concepts/pulumi-cloud/ link resolves: it's an alias on content/docs/iac/concepts/pulumi-cloud.md. That page describes Pulumi Cloud as the state backend with "Role-based access control", teams and organizations as "the primary unit of collaboration", and "Policy as code enforcement applied centrally to every update", which backs the visibility and central-guardrail parts of the claim. The page doesn't use the words "cross-team visibility", and I didn't open the components page linked on the same line.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says "primary unit of collaboration… teams… policy enforcement applied centrally"; the claim paraphrases this as "cross-team visibility… central guardrails".

verdicts.text: Yes. Since SST v3 (the Ion rewrite, shipped mid-2024), `sst deploy` runs through an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls, replacing SST's earlier architecture on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's v3 announcement (dated around August 2024) says "Ion is now officially being released as SST v3" and that it uses "Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation." SST's earlier post says components "are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi."
verdicts.framing_note: SST v3 GA announcement is dated ~Aug 20, 2024; "mid-2024" is a slightly loose but reasonable description.

verdicts.text: SST's components are defined using Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine; SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.
verdicts.evidence: SST's docs say "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi." The SST v3 post says state is "stored locally and backed up to S3", and the bridge README says it connects the Pulumi engine to Terraform providers "using Pulumi's RPC interfaces". Together these imply no Terraform CLI and no Terraform state, though no source says those negatives outright.
verdicts.framing_note: Sources say SST uses Pulumi providers and engine, with Terraform providers bridged through Pulumi. The claim's "does not invoke Terraform CLI / write TF state" is inferred from how the bridge works, not stated. Saying all of SST's "components are defined using Terraform providers" is a bit loose: some Pulumi providers SST uses are not bridged.

verdicts.text: The post at /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ is titled 'AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi' and tells the story of SST's move off CDK from SST's side.
verdicts.evidence: The post's front matter has `title: "AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi"`. Its body tells the story of SST's migration from its team's point of view: "we'll explore why SST moved to Pulumi, what challenges they overcame". It also embeds a video about the limits the SST team hit with CDK and CloudFormation.
verdicts.framing_note: A Pulumi employee (sara-huddleston) wrote the post, but it tells the story from SST's perspective. "From SST's side" is a fair description.

verdicts.text: The pages /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/ and /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/ exist.
verdicts.evidence: Both target pages exist in the repo: content/docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works.md ("title: How Pulumi IaC Works") and content/docs/iac/concepts/automation-api.md ("title: Automation API"). Each file's path maps to the linked URL.

verdicts.text: - [Automation API](/docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/) — how other tools embed Pulumi the same way SST does
verdicts.evidence: The link target exists as content/docs/iac/concepts/automation-api.md (title "Automation API"). The page describes a programmatic SDK "so you can drive the Pulumi engine from within your own application instead of invoking the `pulumi` command from a shell," which fits the link text about embedding Pulumi in other tools.
verdicts.framing_note: This only checks that the link resolves and the page is about embedding Pulumi through Automation API. It does not check whether SST itself uses Automation API.

verdicts.text: [^npm-downloads]: [npm download stats for `sst`](https://api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/last-week/sst), 796,291 downloads for the week of September 5-11, 2026.
verdicts.evidence: The cited endpoint is a rolling "last-week" window. It now returns a later week, so it can't confirm the claimed figure for Sep 5-11: {"downloads":1334575,"start":"2026-09-21","end":"2026-09-27","package":"sst"}. This doesn't contradict the claim, but the citation can't back it. A fixed-range URL (e.g. /downloads/point/2026-09-05:2026-09-11/sst) would.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the source reports a rolling last-7-days count (currently Sep 21-27, 1,334,575), while the claim gives a fixed week (Sep 5-11, 796,291). Different time windows.
verdicts.intuition_flag: A rolling-window URL used as a citation for a fixed-date figure will always drift. Replace it with a date-range endpoint.
